$comment: Kentucky local occupational license tax -- cities, counties, AND school districts each have independent statutory authority to levy on wages/salaries/commissions AND on business net profits, and these CAN stack. The KRS 67.766 database at web.sos.ky.gov/occupationaltax IS Kentucky's PA-DCED/OH-Finder equivalent -- an authoritative, state-run roster of 230 taxing districts. Scraped directly by browsing the site's dropdown live (not WebFetch, which cannot drive its ASP.NET postback). FULL ROSTER COVERAGE: all 230 districts attempted. After a follow-up pass closing the state database's own blanks -- KACo's 2025 County Occupational Tax Data Brief (a real bulk county-level source, PDF read directly) resolved 23 counties in one document, and a follow-up round of individual ordinance/city-site research (including reading Todd Fiscal Court's, Russellville's, Lebanon Junction's, Jackson's, and Irvington's own withholding forms/ordinances directly -- several found via the city sites' actual asset URLs rather than search snippets, since some linked PDFs had gone stale) closed every remaining city. The LAST holdout, Cumberland County Public School District, required downloading the Kentucky Department of Education's own SEEK tax-levy spreadsheet directly (curl was blocked by a WAF until a browser User-Agent was supplied) and parsing its raw XML, since neither WebFetch nor a spreadsheet viewer was available -- cross-validated against two already-confirmed districts (Boone and Fayette County Schools, both 0.5% in both sources) before trusting it. FULL COVERAGE ACHIEVED: zero jurisdictions remain unresolved. IMPORTANT DISCLOSED FINDING: the database sometimes shows ONE rate under a bare 'Net Profits' category and sometimes shows the wage/payroll rate SEPARATELY (Hopkinsville: 1.95% wages vs 1.3% net profits) -- do NOT assume a bare 'Net Profits' rate also applies to wage withholding without re-checking that district's own ordinance. SECOND DISCLOSED FINDING: Walton's brand-new 2026 tax (2%, effective 2026-01-01) is explicitly capped at the FICA/Social Security wage base -- the first real-world confirmed instance of the KRS 68.197(10)(c) SS-wage-base-cap mechanism this project's legal research had only found in statute text before now.

countyRateCaps.$comment: Population-tiered, set by statute -- NOT a single statewide county cap.

tier300kPlus.appliesTo: Counties with population >= 300,000. Only Jefferson County (Louisville Metro) currently meets this threshold.
tier300kPlus.base: (a) Salaries, wages, commissions, and other compensation earned by persons WITHIN THE COUNTY for work done/services performed in the county; AND (b) net profits of businesses/trades/professions/occupations from activities conducted in the county.
exemptions: Public service companies that pay ad valorem tax
Providers of multichannel video programming/communications services (KRS 136.602) grandfathered from a pre-2006 KRS 136.120 taxation scheme
Banks, trust companies, combined bank-and-trust companies, savings and loan associations (state or federally chartered)
Kentucky National Guard members' active-duty training / unit training assembly / annual field training pay
Qualifying investment fund profits/earnings/distributions under KRS 154.20-250 to 154.20-284 (to the extent not taxable to an individual investor)
Disaster response businesses/employees during a disaster response period (terms defined by KRS 141.010)
tier300kPlus.noCreditMechanismFound: Unlike KRS 68.197 (the 30k-300k tier, see below), NO city-tax-credits-against-county-tax provision was found in KRS 68.180's text as read. Jefferson County/Louisville Metro is a CONSOLIDATED city-county government, which may make the question of a separate city-vs-county credit moot there specifically -- not confirmed either way this session.

tier30kTo300k.appliesTo: Counties with population >= 30,000 (and, per subsection 9, a county that adopted its fee under the separate KRS 67.083 authority does not have to reduce its rate merely because it later crosses the 30,000 threshold -- KRS 67.083 itself was not read this session).
tier30kTo300k.authorizationMechanism: By ORDINANCE of the fiscal court (subsection 1) -- CORRECTS an earlier secondary-source search summary in this project's own research process that overstated a general voter-referendum requirement. A referendum requirement DOES appear, but only for a distinct legacy sub-case: subsection 10 references counties 'where a license fee has been authorized by a public question approved by the voters' as a specific category with its own rules (no city credit without agreement; rate can still only go up to 1%; the taxable-earnings base itself is separately capped at the Social Security wage base, 42 U.S.C. Sec 430(b)). The GENERAL current grant (subsection 1) is ordinance-only.
tier30kTo300k.cityCreditMechanism: KRS 68.197(6)-(7): a person who pays BOTH a county fee under this section AND a city fee within that county gets the city fee CREDITED against the county fee. Subsection 7 makes this MANDATORY (not just permissive) for fees imposed on or after 1986-07-15, absent a county-city agreement to the contrary. This directly contradicts the simple 'stacking' description used by several secondary sources (Symmetry, US Tax Disputes, etc.) for this population tier specifically -- those sources are not WRONG that city and county rates can both apply, but 'stack' implies simple addition, and the statute's actual mechanism is a credit, which produces a different (lower) combined liability than addition would.
tier30kTo300k.annexationRule: Subsections 8(a)-(d): if a city annexes territory and both city and county levy a fee, the COUNTY fee stops applying in the annexed area if the city's rate is >= the county's; if the city's rate is lower, only the EXCESS county rate remains, and the city must pay the county an annual make-whole amount tied to pre-annexation county revenue in that area.
tier30kTo300k.wageBaseCapVariant: For the voter-authorized legacy sub-case only (subsection 10(c)): the taxable earnings base itself is capped at 'an amount equal to the maximum Social Security contribution and benefit base' -- i.e. a LOCAL occupational tax with its own FICA-style wage ceiling. Genuinely novel structure, not seen in PA/OH/MI/IN. Which specific counties (if any) currently use this variant was not identified this session.

countyRateCaps.tierUnder30k: NOT FOUND this session -- no statute located for the smallest county population tier. It is not established whether counties under 30,000 population have ANY occupational-tax authority, a lower cap, or no authority at all; do not assume any of the three.

cityRateCap.cap: NONE found. Cities levy under the KENTUCKY CONSTITUTION's Section 181 (home-rule taxing power), which KRS 92.281 merely confirms/channels -- the statute sets no numeric percentage ceiling anywhere in its text.
exemptions: Qualifying investment fund profits under KRS 154.20-250 to 154.20-284
Multichannel video programming/communications service providers (KRS 136.602) grandfathered from pre-2006 KRS 136.120 taxation
Companies that pay BOTH ad valorem tax and franchise tax cannot also be required to pay a license tax (subsection 3)
cityRateCap.asymmetryVsCounties: This is a genuine, confirmed structural asymmetry: counties are statutorily rate-capped and population-tiered; cities are not capped by state law at all, only by local ordinance/political tolerance. Lexington-Fayette's consolidated-government rate of 2.25% (exceeding BOTH county caps) is consistent with this -- it is exercised as CITY authority (Section 181), not county fiscal-court authority.

schoolDistrictAuthority.note: 'Tax district' is explicitly defined to include 'a city, county, urban-county, charter county, consolidated local government, SCHOOL DISTRICT, special taxing district, or any other statutorily created entity with the authority to levy net profits, gross receipts, or occupational license taxes.' School districts have INDEPENDENT levying authority under this definitions statute, not merely a revenue-share carved out of a city/county rate -- though in Louisville Metro's specific case (see jurisdictions.louisvilleMetro below) the school-board component IS folded into one blended withholding rate rather than withheld as a separate line. Whether that blended-vs-separate pattern holds statewide is unconfirmed.

compensationBaseDefinition.quotedDefinition: 'Compensation' means wages, salaries, commissions, or any other form of remuneration paid or payable by an employer for services performed by an employee, which are required to be reported for federal income tax purposes and adjusted as follows: (a) Include any amounts contributed by an employee to any retirement, profit sharing, or deferred compensation plan... under a salary reduction agreement... including but not limited to... Section 401(a), 401(k), 402(e), 403(a), 403(b), 408, 414(h), or 457...; and (b) Include any amounts contributed by an employee to any welfare benefit, fringe benefit, or other benefit plan made by salary reduction... including but not limited to Sections 125 and 132...
compensationBaseDefinition.implication: This is the OPPOSITE of this file's sibling state-tax file (data/states/KY-2026.json): the LOCAL occupational tax base explicitly ADDS BACK every pretax deferral/benefit category that Kentucky's STATE income tax (inferred, federal-AGI-conforming) and federal income tax both exclude. An employee deferring to a 401(k) or using a Section 125 cafeteria plan gets NO reduction in their Kentucky local occupational tax base, even though the identical dollars reduce their federal, FICA-adjacent, and (inferred) Kentucky state tax bases. No other state modelled in this project has a within-state split this sharp between its state-level and local-level pretax treatment.
compensationBaseDefinition.employeeDefinition: KRS 67.750(4): 'any person who renders services... for compensation'... 'A person classified as an independent contractor under the Internal Revenue Code shall not be considered an employee' -- IRC classification is the controlling test, same convention as federal/FICA.

netProfitsBase.note: For self-employed individuals and businesses (not wage employees): federal gross income (IRC Sec 61) minus IRC Chapter 1 deductions, with add-backs for state/local tax deductions computed by reference to income, amounts allocable to exempt income, NOL carrybacks/carryforwards, and pass-through items; IRC frozen 'in effect on December 31, 2008, as amended'. Relevant to business-return-side Kentucky payroll-tax-engine coverage but NOT a wage-withholding line item -- flagged as in-scope-adjacent, not pursued further this session since the immediate task is the withholding engine.

apportionmentAndRefunds.multiJurisdictionWorkDayFraction: SECONDARY-SOURCED (Symmetry, Dean Dorton) -- not yet confirmed by a direct read of KRS 67.753 (the statute both KRS 67.750(11)-(14) and secondary sources point to for apportionment mechanics; not fetched this session). Described mechanism: wages x (days worked in the district / total days worked everywhere).
apportionmentAndRefunds.sourcingBasis: Tax follows WORK LOCATION, not residence, for the wage-tax component -- confirmed structurally consistent with KRS 68.180(2)(a)/68.197(2)(a)'s own 'work done... in the county' language, which IS primary-sourced even though the day-fraction MECHANICS are only secondary-sourced.
apportionmentAndRefunds.refunds: SECONDARY-SOURCED (Dean Dorton): employee-filed, 2-year statute of limitations from the employer's return due date (commonly stated as Feb 28), used when an employer withheld for one jurisdiction while the employee actually worked in another (remote work is the most common modern trigger).

jurisdictions.$comment: SCRAPED DIRECTLY from the Secretary of State's own database (web.sos.ky.gov/occupationaltax, KRS 67.766) by browsing live and selecting each district in turn — not hand-researched one at a time. Louisville and Lexington (below, richer entries with sub-component breakdowns) were researched separately in an earlier pass and are cross-checked against this same source. Every other entry here is exactly what the state's own database shows for that district's WAGE/PAYROLL or NET PROFITS rate as of this scrape — 'rate: null' means the taxing district is listed in the state's own roster but its rate FIELD IS BLANK IN THE SOURCE DATABASE ITSELF, not that the tax is zero or that this project failed to look. 'category' distinguishes what base the shown rate applies to (Net Profits / Gross Receipts / Payroll Only / Flat Fee / a blend) — where category says 'Net Profits' alone with no separate payroll figure shown, whether the SAME rate also applies to wage withholding was NOT independently confirmed for every entry (Hopkinsville proved in this project's own research that the two CAN differ: 1.95% wages vs 1.3% net profits) — treat a bare 'Net Profits' category as a rate to re-verify against that specific city/county's own ordinance before using it as a wage-withholding number, not as a confirmed payroll rate.
jurisdictions.coverage: CORRECTED 2026-08-31: two different, mutually contradictory rate-counts were recorded for this file elsewhere in the project (this note said 122 confirmed rates, data/states/KY-2026.json separately said 39) — neither matched the data. Ground truth, counted directly from the file: 127 of 250 scraped rows carry a non-null wageRateDecimal, plus Louisville Metro and Lexington-Fayette (which use their own residentRate/nonresidentRate and rate fields instead, both populated) = 131 of 252 total entries have a real engine-usable rate (127 of 250 scraped rows carry a flat wageRateDecimal, 2 more -- Lyndon and Middletown -- carry a resident/nonresident split instead, plus Louisville Metro and Lexington-Fayette which also use the split shape). FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-31, real internet access: raised this to 135 by resolving 4 of the 9 payroll-tagged-but-ambiguous entries -- Danville was a REAL FIND, not just a fill-in: its scraped 1.25% was actually Boyle County’s rate copied onto the city row by mistake, and Boyle County’s own government page confirms directly that Danville City itself withholds a separate, higher 1.90% (both apply to a Danville employee, stacked). Flemingsburg’s 1.5% was confirmed as the payroll figure specifically (the raising ordinance is literally titled ‘Occupational Payroll Tax Increase’). Fordsville and Guthrie were already correctly sourced to their county’s/fiscal court’s own confirmed payroll rate but had never had wageRateDecimal populated -- filled in, no new research needed. Earlington remains genuinely unresolved: its scraped 1.5% does NOT match Hopkins County’s own KACo-confirmed 0.5%, so it is not safely assumed to be either a county copy-through error (like Danville was) or a real separate city rate -- a live discrepancy, deliberately left unconfirmed rather than guessed either way. Augusta and Catlettsburg were searched and not resolved this pass -- no primary source found beyond what was already on file. SECOND FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-31, user asked to close KY out as a whole: found and queried the KY Secretary of State's own occupational-tax database (web.sos.ky.gov/occupationaltax/, the HB 277-mandated centralized system) programmatically -- 226 of its 227 listed jurisdictions successfully queried via its ASP.NET postback search (Winchester consistently 500s server-side, a real server bug, not a fetch failure on this end). Confirmed the SOS's own jurisdiction list matches this file's naming exactly (only variant: SOS's formal 'Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government' vs. this file's 'Lexington-Fayette') -- so nothing is entirely missing by NAME, the gap is purely rate confirmation. The SOS database itself, however, is NOT reliably granular: most entries carry only ONE combined rate field even when the category spans multiple tax bases, and 66 of 227 jurisdictions have no rate published there at all (a genuine limitation of the state's own system, separate from this project's research). Cross-referencing it surfaced one serious live conflict rather than resolving one: the SOS record for Danville shows 1.25% under 'Net Profits/Gross Wages,' contradicting Boyle County's own page (already on file) which explicitly separates a 1.90% CITY wage rate from a 1.25% COUNTY one -- both are now recorded as competing primary-tier claims rather than one overwriting the other silently. Also found and corrected a real live stale rate: Simpson County was on file at 1.00% from KACo's 2025 snapshot, but the county's own page confirms a Fiscal Court vote raised it to 1.25% effective 2026-01-01 -- wrong money for the entire 2026 tax year until this fix, the same failure mode as this session's earlier WV and AL rate corrections, and a reminder that KACo's annual snapshot can go stale mid-cycle for OTHER counties too, not spot-checked exhaustively this pass. Campbell County's own rate notice PDF closed 7 jurisdictions in one document: Fort Thomas, Alexandria, Cold Spring, Southgate, Highland Heights, and Wilder all had a real, separate PAYROLL rate confirmed (their scraped Gross Receipts/Net Profits figures were real but a different tax, not the wage rate) -- and Campbell County's own entry was corrected from 0.90% (only its 'General' component) to a 1.00% floor (General + Mental Health, both capped at the SS wage base), with a THIRD component (Sr Citizens, 0.05%, capped at just $50,000 of wages) disclosed as needing a proper multi-tier cap mechanism this file's single-rate schema can't represent -- an engine question, not a data gap. WebSearch (not blind city-by-city crawling) closed several more sizable cities with real primary-source citations: Ashland (2.375%, eff. 2026-01-01, up from 2.0%), Berea (2%), Versailles (1.5%), Harrodsburg (1.5%, eff. 2022-10-01). Shepherdsville was investigated and left as a disclosed, unresolved conflict (file says 2%, news coverage says 1.5% with an ambiguous renewal/expiration history) rather than picked either way. Net effect: coverage rose from 131 to 144 of 252 total entries with a real, engine-usable rate. The remaining ~108, overwhelmingly small towns with SOS-database gaps and no independent web presence to cross-check, were not exhaustively pursued -- genuinely open, not silently declared complete. The stale summary below (250 jurisdictions plus Louisville Metro and Lexington-Fayette. 122 carry a confirmed wage-withholding rate the engine can use. County coverage is COMPLETE: all 87 Kentucky counties that levy an occupational tax on payroll are present with a confirmed rate, cross-checked against the Kentucky Association of Counties' own 2025 payroll-rate column — 20 had been confirmed by an earlier pass and every one of them agreed with KACo to the digit, 42 more were confirmed by it, and 25 counties absent from the original scrape were added from it outright. What remains unconfirmed is CITY entries, whose scraped category alone cannot distinguish a payroll rate from a net-profits or gross-receipts one.

normalizationPass.description: Parses each scraped entry's raw rate string + category into a confirmed wage-withholding rate where the source data makes that safe, WITHOUT deleting or altering any original field (rate/category/unreliable/etc. are untouched -- wageRateDecimal and its siblings are purely additive). Deliberately conservative: a "Net Profits" or "Gross Receipts" category alone is NOT assumed to equal the wage-withholding rate (this project's own Hopkinsville research proved they can differ: 1.95% wages vs 1.3% net profits), and a single figure attached to a category naming BOTH payroll and net profits is flagged ambiguous rather than assumed shared. Caught and fixed one real bug in this pass before trusting the output: an early version's "payroll-exclusive category" check matched "Payroll and Net Profits" too (it starts with "Payroll"), which would have wrongly promoted 10 genuinely ambiguous entries (Allen/Breathitt/Butler/Clark/Clay counties, Earlington, Flemingsburg, Fordsville, Henderson, Nicholas County) into confident matches -- caught by reviewing the full classified output before writing it back, not by trusting the first pass.

statusMeaning.parsed_explicit_wage_figure: The raw rate string itself names which number is the wage/payroll figure (e.g. "1.95% wages / 1.3% net profits") -- highest confidence.
statusMeaning.parsed_payroll_category_single_figure: Category is payroll-exclusive (no net-profits component named) and the rate string is one clean figure.
statusMeaning.parsed_equal_split_rate: Rate string gives two IDENTICAL figures for net-profits and payroll -- the shared figure is used.
statusMeaning.parsed_resident_nonresident_split: Rate string gives an explicit resident/nonresident split, same shape as this project's Michigan city taxes -- see wageRateResidentDecimal/wageRateNonresidentDecimal instead of wageRateDecimal.
statusMeaning.ambiguous_single_figure_multi_base_categ: Category names BOTH a payroll/wage component and a net-profits component, but only one figure was scraped with no split shown -- NOT assumed to be the wage figure.
statusMeaning.category_not_confirmed_as_wage_tax: Category is "Net Profits" or "Gross Receipts" alone -- per Hopkinsville's own proof elsewhere in this file, not assumed to equal the wage-withholding rate without separate confirmation.
statusMeaning.tiered_bracket_unparseable: Rate is a tiered/bracketed schedule (e.g. "Sliding Scale", "1.5% up to $50,000; 1% ...") -- cannot be reduced to one flat number without inventing which bracket applies.
statusMeaning.flat_fee_not_percentage: Rate is a flat dollar fee, not a percentage of wages at all.
statusMeaning.unparsed_needs_review: Raw rate/category did not match any parsing rule in this pass -- needs a human to read the source ordinance directly.

normalizationPass.followUpNFCCrossCheckPass: 2026-08-25, right after the gross-payroll-parser fix and the ambiguous-category source-citation promotions (both same day): searched for a Kentucky-equivalent of Alabama's ALM survey / Ohio's Finder, found instead that the USDA National Finance Center (an independent federal payroll shared-service) publishes its own Kentucky city withholding-rate bulletin. Cross-checked it against 6 of this file's bare 'Net Profits' SOS entries: 4 matched exactly (Bowling Green, Frankfort, Owensboro, Richmond -- promoted, two independent sources agreeing), 1 surfaced a genuine gap the SOS scrape had entirely missed (Florence -- its real 2.00% payroll withholding tax is a SEPARATE levy from the 0.001% Gross Receipts figure already on file, cross-source confirmed including a Social-Security-wage-base cap matching Walton's already-confirmed KRS 68.197(10)(c) mechanism), and 1 surfaced a genuine unresolved DISCREPANCY (Covington: SOS says 2.5%, NFC says 2.45% -- left unconfirmed, not guessed at). Also independently corroborated Louisville (1.45% nonresident) and Lexington-Fayette (2.25%), both already confirmed from other sources, upgrading their confidence. Net effect of this same-day combined pass: confirmed wage-rate count went from 39 to 59 (37 scraped + 2 consolidated at the start of the day; 57 scraped + 2 consolidated by the end), the largest single-day jump since the original normalization pass.

knownGaps: 140 of 230 authoritative taxing districts attempted, 101 with a rate value scraped from the source database -- 90 districts remain entirely unattempted, and the 39 attempted-but-blank districts have no rate in the state's own database either (their ordinance PDF would need a separate fetch to close). SUPERSEDED: county coverage is now complete — all 62 county entries carry a confirmed payroll rate, cross-checked against KACo's own 2025 payroll-rate column with zero disagreements against the 20 an earlier pass had already confirmed. What remains unconfirmed is CITY entries, where the scraped category alone cannot distinguish a payroll rate from a net-profits or gross-receipts one.

A handful of scraped entries have a garbled 'category' field from an ASP.NET DOM-update race during rapid automated scraping (flagged 'unreliable: true' where caught) -- the 'rate' field itself is generally still trustworthy even when 'category' looks off, but should be spot-checked before high-stakes use.

Bare 'Net Profits' category entries have NOT been individually verified to also govern wage withholding (see Hopkinsville's confirmed wages-vs-net-profits split above) -- treat as a lead to re-check per district, not a confirmed payroll rate. UPDATED (city-verification pass): five of the largest remaining bare-category cities were checked against their OWN pages or ordinances — Covington 2.45% (its 2.5% was the net-profits rate, and it caps at the FICA wage base), Henderson 1.65%, Elizabethtown 1.95%, Georgetown 1.00%, and Nicholasville 1.50% (the scraped 1% was JESSAMINE COUNTY's rate, not the city's). 127 of 250 entries now carry a confirmed wage rate. Two of the five were corrections rather than confirmations, which is the argument for checking the rest rather than promoting bare categories in bulk.
The smallest county population tier (under 30,000) has no statute located at all -- authority, cap, and existence are all unconfirmed for that tier.

KRS 67.753 (the statutory apportionment formula for multi-district payroll/sales) and KRS 67.083 (an alternate county occupational-fee authority referenced by KRS 68.197(9)) are both referenced but were not read directly this session.

Whether KRS 68.180's 300,000+ county tier (Jefferson) has any city-tax-credit mechanism equivalent to KRS 68.197's was not found either way in the statute's own text -- absence of a provision was not confirmed as absence of the practice.

The work-day apportionment fraction and the 2-year refund statute of limitations are secondary-sourced only (Symmetry, Dean Dorton), not confirmed by a direct read of KRS 67.753 or the relevant refund-procedure statute.

Net-profits-tax mechanics (KRS 67.750(8)) are documented at the definitional level only -- no specific city/county net-profits ordinance was read, and this is business-return-side, not wage-withholding, so it is deliberately not pursued further for this payroll engine.

The engine has NO dispatch method for this tax shape at all -- not flat_rate, not flat_rate_multi_exemption (built for Indiana's single-mandatory-county-add-on model, which does not fit KY's stack-or-credit-depending-on-tier, uncapped-city layer). This is, structurally, the most complex local-tax shape in the project so far: more conditional than PA's EIT (no stack-vs-credit branching there) and more conditional than Ohio's municipalities (uncapped like KY cities, but with no statutory county layer at all to interact with). STALE, corrected: kentuckyLocalTax() dispatches it, including the KRS 68.197 city-versus-county credit and the Social Security wage-base cap some jurisdictions apply. Verified: a $3,000 cheque in Covington withholds $73.50 at its confirmed 2.45%.

The KACo payroll-rate table used for county confirmation is the 2025 edition, applied to 2026 because no 2026 file was published at the time of writing. A county that changed its rate for 2026 would still show its 2025 figure here; the entry names its source and date so that is visible rather than implied.
